text:
Jen: Thinking out loud — current autoscaler feels too one-sided. Operators inject capacity but tenants only emit demand. Can we design a tiny "offer/accept" SLA negotiation so the operator can *advertise* transient capabilities and tenants can accept/decline?
Rahul: Interesting. Like operator says: "I can guarantee X qps at SLO for Y minutes" and tenant either binds or ignores? :thinking_face:
Sam: That would let us surface burst lanes without hard reservations. Operator could advertise short-lived offers backed by spare GPUs.
Emily: We should be explicit about pricing and preemption contract in the offer. Tenants need an atomic accept that returns a lease id.
Jen: Exactly. Sketch of API: operator => Offer { capacity, duration, preemptible, price, cancelable_after } tenant => Accept(offer_id) => Lease(lease_id, start_ts, end_ts). If not accepted, offer expires.
Rahul: A couple of tradeoffs:
- Complexity: creates extra control-plane chatter and state to reconcile offers.
- Fairness: need priority rules so offers don't always go to high-paying tenants.
- Safety: ensure we never double-allocate the same GPU.
Sam: Implementation idea: offers are optimistic — they reserve a tiny token (non-gpu) in the ledger. Only on accept do we turn token -> actual allocation. That keeps offers cheap to emit.
Emily: Also add a "constraints" field to offers so tenants can filter: model_shape, min_seq_len, perf_profile. Otherwise noisy offers will be rejected by everyone.
Jen: Example offer (proto-ish):
```
Offer {
  id: "off-2026-03-01-001"
  capacity: 16 gpus
  duration_secs: 300
  perf_profile: "llama-2-13b-fast"
  preemptible: true
  price_multiplier: 0.6
  cancel_window_secs: 30
}
```
Rahul: On accept semantics — we should return a lease token that encodes soft vs hard reservation. Soft = best-effort, can be evicted with Xs notice. Hard = backed by actual pre-provisioned GPU and only reclaimed if tenant cancels.
Sam: For billing, soft leases charge only on usage; hard leases charge a time-based commit. Also record a TTL in the lease for automatic expiry to avoid leaks.
Emily: Observability: every offer/accept/cancel should be visible in Console with a small timeline. Traces should link request -> offer -> lease -> eviction.
Jen: Where to put this logic? Operator-side seems natural for offer generation (it knows spare capacity), but lease lifecycle needs a reconciler in the orchestration layer.
Rahul: Agree. Operator generates offers and publishes them to the control-plane topic (kafka). Orchestration reconciler listens and writes offers into the intent store. Accept calls go to orchestration API which does the token->alloc transition with CAS.
Sam: Edge-case: simultaneous accept from two tenants for the same offer. Use CAS on the offer token; first to CAS wins and the other gets an offer_rejected with reason "claimed".
Emily: Eviction policy: offers can include max_preemptions_per_minute to rate-limit churn for tenants who accept many short offers.
orch-bot: deploy 4970012345: offer-proto sketch pushed to proto-repo at refs/heads/offer-proto; ACL: eng-runtime.
Jen: Security note — offers must not leak capacity shapes that expose infra details. Obfuscate exact GPU ids and just advertise logical capacity and perf buckets.
Rahul: One more optimization: if a tenant repeatedly accepts offers, the orchestrator can propose a conversion to a hard reservation with a one-click flow (and commit pricing). That improves UX and reduces churn.
Sam: Could also surface "safety margin" in offers: operator promises X usable gpus but keeps H headroom for infra noise. Make H tunable per operator region.
Emily: For rollout, start with a read-only offer feed and a simulated accept in dry-run mode. Then enable actual accept for a small set of tenants with canary limits.
Jen: Action items: 1) Rahul — write a minimal proto + CAS semantics doc. 2) Sam — sketch reconciler state transitions (offer -> token -> lease -> alloc). 3) Emily — console mockups for offers panel. 4) I'll add a short postmortem-style checklist for safety hooks.
Rahul: I'll drop a PR with proto+sample JSON and a small finite-state machine diagram later today.
Sam: I'll start on the reconciler pseudo-code, keeping idempotency first.
Emily: I'll mock the UI and the observability events we need.
Jen: Sweet. If we keep offers cheap and stateless-ish we get burst capacity without blowing up the control plane. :+1:
